title: Atomic-resolution imaging of a single non-crystalline molecule before destruction

concept.text: The innovation is to determine a molecule’s atomic structure without arranging copies into a crystal or immobilizing them in vitreous ice. An intense femtosecond X-ray pulse would record diffraction from an individually exposed molecule before radiation damage destroys its useful structural information. Computational reconstruction would turn the scattered intensities into a three-dimensional structure, locating atoms rather than only revealing the molecule’s overall shape. This diffraction-before-destruction approach is scientifically motivated, but atomic reconstruction of non-crystalline molecules remains a future goal in the supplied evidence.

Two levels of capability must be distinguished within this goal. Atomic reconstruction from diffraction patterns collected from many separately destroyed molecules could establish the structure of a sufficiently consistent molecular state. A complete atomic snapshot of one unique individual molecule from one exposure would be a stronger achievement. The documented approach combines signals and orientations from many molecules; its progress and the proposed ensemble benchmark do not establish the stronger individual-molecule capability.

Unlike Bragg crystallography, which uses periodic repetition, this approach must recover structure from the continuous diffraction of a non-periodic object. Each exposure provides limited information at an initially unknown molecular orientation. Recovering a three-dimensional structure therefore involves identifying useful patterns, determining their orientations, resolving structural differences and recovering the phase information needed to form an image without supplying the sought atomic structure as the answer.

significance.text: Validated atomic reconstruction without crystallization or cryo-fixation would materially extend structural biology. Suitable molecules that resist crystallization could become accessible to atomic structural study, and measurements would avoid constraints imposed by a crystal lattice. Femtosecond exposures would also provide a route to comparing rapidly changing molecular states, provided those states can be prepared and sampled reliably.

The comparison with cryo-electron microscopy needs care. Cryo-EM can already recover atomic-scale structural detail by combining images of molecules immobilized in vitreous ice; the supplied erythrocruorin work reports a 3.06 Å cryo-EM reconstruction as a comparison. The prospective advance here is the combination of lattice-free molecular diffraction, ultrashort exposure and measurement without cryo-fixation. It would not automatically make every small molecule or heterogeneous sample reconstructable: those extensions require enough signal and a demonstrated ability to distinguish and recover the relevant states.

Time-resolved measurements could reveal structural changes that a lattice constrains or suppresses. However, a short exposure alone does not produce a molecular movie. Experiments would still need suitable preparation, triggering where applicable, controlled delays and sufficient sampling of each state. Because each exposure destroys its specimen, a sequence assembled from fresh molecules would describe reproducibly prepared states rather than follow the trajectory of the same individual molecule.

Conditional downstream possibilities include explaining solution-phase catalysis and informing drug design through structures of relevant intermediates or ligand-bound states. These applications additionally require delivery, preservation and identification of the chemically relevant state. An image of an isolated molecule that has changed during preparation would not by itself establish its behavior in solution or in a cell. Intracellular ensembles of intrinsically disordered proteins remain outside this entry’s scope.

missing_breakthrough.text: The central unsolved capability is reliable atomic reconstruction from the weak continuous diffraction of non-crystalline molecules without assuming their atomic model. A molecule scatters few useful photons, especially at the fine spatial scales needed to distinguish atomic features. The exposure must collect sufficient information before radiation-induced changes compromise it. The original simulations support physical plausibility, while the later work retains near-atomic and atomic molecular imaging as goals rather than demonstrated outcomes.

Signal collection and sample delivery must improve together. Scattering from the delivery environment and other background can obscure the molecular signal, while inefficient delivery limits the number of useful single-molecule patterns. More patterns help only when they contain recoverable information and represent states that can be combined appropriately. The limiting factor is condition-dependent: a 2025 simulation study found that experimental geometry limited improvement at 1.2 keV even when background and dataset size were varied, so background and delivery cannot be assigned a universal dominance over all other errors.

Reconstruction must solve unknown orientations and missing phases while separating conformations instead of blurring them together. Molecular deformation during delivery introduces an additional problem: patterns may come from particles that no longer share the intended structure. The erythrocruorin preprint uses classification, averaging and imposed D6 symmetry, and identifies heterogeneity associated with gas-phase compaction as a likely explanation for its poorer three-dimensional resolution. Reaching atomic detail will require sufficient structural consistency or sufficiently effective state separation, with validation that any structural constraints have not imposed the desired answer.

For the stronger goal of reconstructing one unique individual, information from other copies cannot simply substitute for missing views of that specimen. The supplied approach obtains three-dimensional information by combining many orientations across different molecules. A complete atomic structure from one destructive exposure would therefore require an additional demonstrated means of acquiring or recovering enough information about that individual; success at ensemble reconstruction would leave this barrier unresolved.

current_state.text: Neutze and colleagues’ Nature paper, published on 17 August 2000, used computer simulations to predict that intense femtosecond X-ray pulses could yield useful structural information from single protein molecules and small assemblies before destruction. This was a theoretical feasibility result, not an experimental atomic reconstruction. The supplied review had access to a subscription preview supporting that distinction, rather than the complete paper.

Ekeberg and colleagues’ paper published on 12 January 2024 reported an interpretable diffraction pattern from a single GroEL complex. The radially averaged signal reached the background near 6 nm, or about 60 Å. This measures the signal extent of the pattern; it is not a demonstrated atomic resolution or a complete three-dimensional reconstruction. The article states that its phase-retrieved map allowed no further structural conclusions. The supplied review assessed the full main text but did not inspect the figure images. Although the originally cited repository copy was not captured, the retained publisher article independently supports this result.

A Nature Communications paper published on 1 February 2024 described single-particle imaging resolutions as still far from atomic. The same paper demonstrated atomic structures of crystalline GaAs and GaP using a different, Kossel-based method. That crystalline achievement is relevant evidence of progress in diffraction methods, but it does not demonstrate atomic reconstruction of a non-crystalline molecule.

A Scientific Reports study published on 12 August 2025 used simulations to examine reconstruction limits under different experimental conditions. It supports the importance of background reduction, useful dataset size and experimental geometry, and distinguishes reconstructions that reveal large-scale macromolecular changes from those sufficient for direct atomic modeling. Its numerical results are simulated outcomes, not experimental completion of the molecular imaging goal. The supplied review assessed the complete ten-page main article, extending the earlier research’s abstract-only treatment.

An arXiv preprint submitted on 8 October 2026, with a 24 October revision reported in the supplied research, describes erythrocruorin imaging. It reports selected two-dimensional class reconstructions to about 15 Å and three-dimensional images to approximately 20–30 Å, with anisotropic three-dimensional resolution. These reconstructions combine many single-particle patterns: two-dimensional classes contain roughly a few hundred patterns on average, and three-dimensional reconstruction combines thousands, with D6 symmetry imposed. The authors identify heterogeneity associated with gas-phase compaction as a likely explanation for the resolution gap between the two-dimensional and three-dimensional results, rather than establishing it as the sole cause.

The supplied review’s extraction of the erythrocruorin manuscript includes the relevant main text and methods but ends during page 77. It supports reporting the stated results and reconstruction procedures, while leaving a full figure and supplementary-material audit incomplete. The available arXiv metadata establishes the October submission, but does not establish whether a peer-reviewed version existed by 1 November 2026. Across the supplied dated results, the remaining gap is between nanometer-scale imaging of large complexes and validated atomic reconstruction of non-crystalline molecular states. Completeness of the literature record through that cutoff was not established, so these results cannot support an exhaustive claim about every contemporary development.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed ensemble demonstration, not an established standard: reconstruct several non-crystalline molecular species from hard-X-ray diffraction patterns collected from individually exposed molecules, including at least one species under 100 kDa. The recovered detail should locate side chains and bound ligands without supplying the target atomic model during reconstruction. Combining many molecules would be permitted, provided their structural consistency or separation into distinct states is demonstrated. The number of targets and the under-100-kDa boundary are proposed tests of breadth and signal performance, not published completion thresholds.
completion_criteria.label: Reconstruct multiple species atomically without target models, including one under 100 kDa

completion_criteria.text: Proposed validation should include diffraction data withheld from reconstruction and comparison with an independently determined structure withheld until evaluation. Reports should distinguish directional resolution, local interpretability and atomic-model accuracy, and disclose symmetry assumptions, other structural constraints, classification decisions and rejected data. Independent repetitions using new sample preparations and datasets, ideally by another group or facility, would strengthen confidence that the result is reproducible and does not depend on the target answer being encoded in the reconstruction.
completion_criteria.label: Validate reconstructions against withheld diffraction and independently determined structures

completion_criteria.text: Proposed time-resolved tier: obtain a validated pair of atomic reconstructions at controlled delays for a suitable non-crystallizable specimen, using fresh molecules at each delay. Demonstrate preparation or triggering of the intended chemical state, delay control and a structural difference distinguishable from delivery-induced changes or reconstruction uncertainty. This would establish a reproducible comparison between molecular states, not a trajectory of the same destroyed molecule.
completion_criteria.label: Validate paired atomic reconstructions at controlled delays using fresh molecules

completion_criteria.text: The stronger individual-molecule goal requires its own proposed demonstration: recover and independently validate the complete three-dimensional atomic structure of one unique molecule from its exposure, with a clear accounting of information supplied by measurements, prior assumptions and other specimens. Ensemble success should be reported separately from this stronger result. Nanometer-scale images, one oriented diffraction pattern or a reconstruction that needs the target atomic model would not satisfy the atomic reconstruction criteria.
completion_criteria.label: Stronger: Independently validate one molecule’s complete atomic structure from its exposure

completion_criteria.text: Proposed practical boundaries should be reported alongside successful structures: molecular size, conformational variability, sample consumption, useful-pattern throughput, background conditions, delivery-induced changes and state-preparation requirements. Results on a finite set of targets would demonstrate that tested breadth; they would not establish applicability to every molecule, arbitrary heterogeneity or all physiological states.
completion_criteria.label: Report practical imaging boundaries and limits of tested applicability

related_concepts.text: The closest methodological overlaps are coherent diffractive imaging, XFEL single-particle imaging and time-resolved structural biology. These supply the diffraction, reconstruction and timing foundations of CRX-01. Atomic reconstruction of GaAs/GaP crystals is a distinct achievement because periodic crystalline specimens and the Kossel method do not resolve the information problem for isolated non-crystalline molecules.

Roster-based comparison: CRX-08, “Ab initio atomic structure of matter that exists only once,” is especially close to the stronger unique-individual goal. CRX-01’s ensemble milestone can use many separately exposed molecules representing a consistent state, whereas a specimen that exists only once cannot rely on repeated copies of that specimen. CRX-06, “Atomic movies of elementary chemical steps without a photo-trigger,” overlaps the dynamic ambition but adds a distinct requirement for observing chemical steps without a photo-trigger; a controlled-delay pair under CRX-01 would not automatically meet it.

Roster-based comparison: CRX-02, “Chemically complete atomic structures of bulk amorphous solids,” and CRX-04, “Atomic ensembles measured from total X-ray scattering,” also address structural information beyond a simple periodic average. Their stated targets are bulk amorphous matter and atomic ensembles, respectively, rather than isolated molecular diffraction before destruction. CRX-05, “Experimental many-electron quantum states of real crystals,” and CRX-09, “Protonation state as a routine crystallographic observable,” seek electronic or chemical information that an atomic coordinate reconstruction alone would not necessarily supply.

Roster-based comparison: CRX-10, “Laboratory sources that do facility-class coherent X-ray crystallography,” concerns source capability and access, which could support diffraction experiments but would not by itself solve molecular reconstruction. CRX-11, “Diffraction-quality crystals of arbitrary macromolecules on demand,” addresses sample preparation through crystallization, offering a different route to structural access. CRX-12, “Continuous atomic-resolution crystallography inside working devices and static extreme environments,” concerns sustained measurements in operating or extreme conditions, with different specimen and exposure requirements from destructive molecular snapshots.

Roster-based comparison: CRX-03, “Chemical-accuracy prediction of which molecular crystal will form,” CRX-07, “Predictive experimental selection of a chosen crystal form,” and CRX-13, “A growth rulebook that suppresses defects, twins, and disorder in arbitrary crystals,” concern prediction or control of crystalline materials. They remain separate from CRX-01’s lattice-free measurement goal. The earlier research’s assertion that CRX-01 equals historical item 7 cannot be checked because that historical item was not supplied; the current roster’s CRX-07 concerns crystal-form selection and should not be treated as that historical equivalence.

change_log.change: Preserved CRX-01’s ID, title and ultimate individual-molecule ambition while separating ensemble atomic reconstruction from a complete atomic structure of one unique molecule.
change_log.reason: The documented method and original proposed benchmark combine many destructive exposures and therefore do not establish the stronger capability.

change_log.change: Made access to small or heterogeneous specimens conditional on demonstrated signal and state-recovery performance.
change_log.reason: Lattice-free femtosecond imaging does not automatically solve weak scattering or arbitrary conformational heterogeneity.

change_log.change: Clarified time-resolved comparisons as measurements of fresh molecules prepared at controlled delays.
change_log.reason: Destructive exposures cannot follow the same molecule through successive frames, and ultrashort exposure alone does not establish chemical-state preparation or timing.

change_log.change: Retained the 2000 prediction, 2024 GroEL signal limit and 2026 erythrocruorin resolution ranges while identifying what each result actually measures.
change_log.reason: Simulations, single-pattern signal extent, two-dimensional class reconstructions and three-dimensional atomic structures are different levels of evidence.

change_log.change: Added the erythrocruorin reconstruction’s averaging, imposed D6 symmetry, anisotropic resolution and qualified compaction explanation.
change_log.reason: These details explain both the reported progress and the limits on interpreting it as individual-molecule or unrestricted heterogeneous-state imaging.

change_log.reason: The crystalline Kossel experiment does not complete CRX-01 despite demonstrating atomic structural recovery in another setting.

change_log.change: Expanded proposed completion tests to include held-out diffraction validation, independent structural comparison, reproducibility and practical operating boundaries.
change_log.reason: These proposals make atomic reconstruction assessable while keeping the under-100-kDa target and other thresholds distinct from established standards.

change_log.change: Explained relationships to all other supplied roster entries and left the historical item 7 equivalence unconfirmed.

unresolved_issues: Whether additional results or a peer-reviewed erythrocruorin publication existed by 1 November 2026 remains unknown; the supplied freshness search record was empty.
The erythrocruorin extraction ends during page 77, preventing a complete manuscript, figure and supplementary-material assessment from the supplied review.
Gas-phase compaction is a likely explanation for erythrocruorin’s poorer three-dimensional resolution, but its contribution relative to other causes remains unresolved.
Atomic reconstruction of smaller targets, recovery of heterogeneous states and preservation of chemically relevant states require demonstrations beyond the supplied nanometer-scale results.
A complete atomic structure of one unique individual from one exposure remains a stronger unresolved capability than the proposed ensemble milestone.
The historical item 7 equivalence cannot be checked without that item’s wording; the supplied CRX-07 roster entry does not establish the asserted identity.

brief.title: Seeing a single molecule’s atoms before it is destroyed
possible: Researchers could locate atoms in molecules that resist forming crystals, without freezing them in ice. An extremely short X-ray flash would capture a scattering pattern before destroying the molecule. Computers would turn those patterns into a structure.
Combining patterns from many matching molecules could reveal their shared structure. The stronger goal is a complete atomic picture of one unique molecule from its own exposure.
why: Biologists could study structures without the constraints of a crystal’s repeating arrangement. Comparing rapidly changing molecular states could help explain how reactions work and inform drug design.

sources.showed: Their computer simulations predicted that sufficiently short, intense X-ray exposures could capture structural information before a protein molecule was destroyed.
sources.quote: experiments using very high X-ray dose rates and ultrashort exposures may provide useful structural information before radiation damage destroys the sample.
sources.cited_for: The physical basis for collecting useful information before destruction.
sources.not_established: Simulations did not demonstrate an experimental atomic structure.

sources.showed: They measured an interpretable X-ray scattering pattern from an individual GroEL protein complex. The pattern revealed its approximate orientation.
sources.quote: From the pattern, it is possible to determine the approximate orientation of the protein.
sources.cited_for: The approach works at the scale of an individual protein complex.
sources.not_established: A scattering pattern did not provide a complete three-dimensional structure or locate atoms.

sources.showed: They determined atomic structures of gallium arsenide and gallium phosphide crystals using a single X-ray pulse.
sources.quote: In these demonstration experiments, we collected Kossel patterns of good-quality crystals of GaP and GaAs and could determine both the amplitudes and the phases of the structure factors.
sources.cited_for: An atomic structure can be recovered from an ultrashort exposure of a crystal.
sources.not_established: The method relied on crystals and did not solve the problem for an isolated molecule.

sources.showed: In a preprint, they combined patterns from many erythrocruorin protein complexes into three-dimensional images. They assumed matching repeated parts to help reconstruct the structure.
sources.quote:
here we demonstrate imaging of a single molecular 
complex, the giant-hemoglobin erythrocruorin (Ery) with X-ray laser pulses.
sources.cited_for: Three-dimensional imaging has reached a large protein complex without crystallization.
sources.not_established: The images did not resolve individual atoms or recover one unique molecule’s complete structure.

sources.who: Tong You, Johan Bielecki and Filipe R. N. C. Maia
sources.showed: Their simulations showed that unwanted scattering from delivery gas can obscure molecular detail. More useful patterns and suitable experimental geometry also affect reconstruction.
sources.quote: We observe that background significantly impacts the achievable resolution, particularly when the signal strength is comparable to the background.
sources.cited_for: Signal quality and experimental conditions determine how much detail can be recovered.
sources.not_established: Simulated improvements did not demonstrate atomic imaging of a molecule.

shown: Paul Lourdu Xavier and colleagues’ preprint reports three-dimensional images assembled from thousands of separately exposed protein complexes. These reveal overall structure rather than atoms, and their detail varies with direction.
missing: Experiments have yet to recover atomic detail from molecules outside crystals without supplying the target atomic structure.
Delivery and measurement must preserve the intended molecular state while collecting enough useful scattering.
Reconstruction must distinguish different molecular shapes rather than blur them together.
One destructive exposure must provide enough information to recover a unique molecule’s complete structure.

milestones.label: Several molecular species yield atomic structures without target models
milestones.explanation: Several species, including one below 100 kilodaltons, a measure of molecular mass, would reveal protein side branches and attached molecules without target models. This would test breadth and performance with weaker signals.

milestones.label: Independent tests confirm the recovered structures
milestones.explanation: Reconstructions would match unused scattering data and independently determined structures hidden until evaluation. This would test accuracy without letting the expected answer shape the result.

milestones.label: Controlled delays reveal atomic changes between molecular states
milestones.explanation: Fresh molecules would yield validated atomic structures at paired, controlled delays, with changes separated from preparation effects. This would establish a reproducible comparison of changing states.

milestones.label: One molecule’s exposure yields its complete atomic structure
milestones.explanation: A unique molecule’s exposure would yield its complete, independently validated structure, with assumptions and information from other specimens accounted for. This would establish the stronger individual-molecule capability.

milestones.label: Successful imaging comes with measured practical limits
milestones.explanation: Successful structures would come with measured limits on size, shape variation, sample use, collection rate and preparation conditions. This would define which molecules and states the method can handle.

uncertain: How much does compaction during gas delivery explain the poorer three-dimensional detail in erythrocruorin images?
Can smaller molecules and mixtures of different molecular shapes yield enough information for atomic reconstruction?
The proposed breadth and size benchmarks are tests to aim for, rather than agreed standards for success.

page.title: 3 Å X-ray single-particle imaging of non-crystalline molecules
page.definition: Three-dimensional electron density, the spatial distribution of electrons, is reconstructed at 3 Å (0.3 nm) resolution for non-crystalline molecules from femtosecond X-ray diffraction. Each exposure records one molecular copy before destruction, and reconstruction combines copies measured in different orientations without freezing them in vitreous ice.

goal.need: Neutze and colleagues estimated a conventional radiation-damage barrier of about 200 X-ray photons/Å² at 12 keV. The LCLS workshop identified conformational changes on nanosecond-to-millisecond timescales as a reason to pursue crystal-free femtosecond imaging.

statements.body: Linac Coherent Light Source single-particle imaging workshop
statements.quote: Define an R&D roadmap to achieve 3D atomic-resolution single-particle imaging using X-rays
statements.context: The published roadmap records the charge given to the workshop held in March 2014.

statements.quote: This proposal aims to develop the science and technology to make ultrafast single-protein imaging a reality
statements.context: Objective of grant agreement 101088426, signed on 7 December 2023.

completion.title: A non-crystalline biomolecule’s three-dimensional X-ray map reaches 3 Å resolution.
completion.criterion: Experimentally reconstruct the three-dimensional electron density of a non-crystalline biomolecule at 3 Å (0.3 nm) resolution or finer using femtosecond X-ray single-particle diffraction before destruction. Recover scattering phases from the measured intensities. Reconstruction combines separately exposed molecular copies in different orientations, measured without crystallization or vitrification. Establish the resolution of the reconstructed electron density.
completion.set_by: LCLS, Strategic Facility Development Plan, November 2020, section on single-particle imaging, reaffirming the 2015 workshop roadmap.
completion.threshold_quote: reaching 3 Å resolution of biological objects
completion.basis: LCLS supplies a numerical endpoint for its molecular-imaging programme. Published SPI methodology obtains three-dimensional structure by combining exposures of multiple particles in different orientations. This completion test follows that ensemble-imaging scope and concerns their shared molecular structure.

milestones.title: A destructive femtosecond X-ray exposure yields an image with no measurable radiation damage.
milestones.criterion: Recover an image of a non-periodic test object by phase retrieval from one destructive exposure, with no measurable damage in the reconstructed image. Chapman and colleagues reported this laboratory demonstration on 12 November 2006 using one 25 fs pulse containing approximately 10¹² photons at 32 nm wavelength.
milestones.set_by: Coherent diffractive imaging community, experimental diffraction-before-destruction demonstration published by Chapman and colleagues in 2006.
milestones.threshold_quote: shows no measurable damage, and is reconstructed at the diffraction-limited resolution.

milestones.title: One protein complex yields an X-ray diffraction pattern with a recoverable approximate orientation.
milestones.criterion: Record an interpretable femtosecond diffraction pattern from one isolated protein complex and determine its approximate orientation. Ekeberg and colleagues reported this result for one GroEL complex, approximately 14 nm in diameter, on 12 January 2024.
milestones.set_by: European XFEL–Uppsala collaboration, published single-protein diffraction-before-destruction demonstration by Ekeberg and colleagues.
milestones.threshold_quote: From the pattern, it is possible to determine the approximate orientation of the protein.

milestones.title: A non-crystalline molecular complex yields a three-dimensional X-ray map at a few nanometres.
milestones.criterion: Reconstruct a molecular complex’s three-dimensional electron density at a few nanometres using single-copy exposures. A preprint submitted on 8 October 2026 reports photosystem I at 3.8 nm from 32,788 patterns. The erythrocruorin preprint revised on 24 October 2026 reports anisotropic 3D resolution of about 20–30 Å from thousands of patterns, assuming sixfold symmetry and perpendicular twofold axes. Both reports are preprints without verified peer-reviewed versions.
milestones.set_by: LCLS 2015 roadmap, steps 5 and 8. The few-nanometre benchmark was introduced for larger test objects, followed by a full SPI experiment on a suitable small object.
milestones.threshold_quote: Seeking success at a few nanometer resolution

milestones.title: A non-crystalline molecular complex yields a three-dimensional X-ray map finer than 1 nm.
milestones.criterion: Experimentally reconstruct a molecular complex’s three-dimensional electron density at sub-nanometre resolution, meaning finer than 1 nm. The GroEL simulations published on 12 August 2025 reached approximately 1.1 nm using 100,000 simulated patterns at 6 keV.
milestones.set_by: SPI community’s sub-nanometre reconstruction objective, described by Bielecki, Maia and Mancuso in 2020 and retained by You, Bielecki and Maia in 2025.
milestones.threshold_quote: sub-nanometer reconstructions of non-crystalline biological and non-biological samples

milestones.title: A complete molecular diffraction dataset reaches 3 Å in three dimensions.
milestones.criterion: Assemble molecular diffraction patterns with recovered relative orientations into a three-dimensional intensity volume with sufficient sampling and integrated signal to 3 Å. This applies the published complete-dataset criterion to the LCLS resolution target and supplies the experimental volume for phase retrieval. The erythrocruorin preprint reports merged reciprocal-space intensity extending beyond 20 Å.
milestones.set_by: SPI complete-dataset criterion published by Bielecki, Maia and Mancuso in 2020, evaluated at the LCLS programme’s 3 Å target.
milestones.threshold_quote: Fourier space is sufficiently sampled with enough integrated signal to a given resolution.

not_found: Searches of LCLS roadmaps, ERC project objectives and SPI literature found no published acceptance test for complete atomic reconstruction of one unique molecule from one exposure.
The LCLS roadmap and development plan supplied no prescribed resolution-validation metric or numerical acceptance cutoff for their 3 Å target.
Searches by title and arXiv identifier found no peer-reviewed versions of the two molecular-imaging preprints submitted on 8 October 2026.
The full erythrocruorin PDF revised on 24 October 2026 exceeded the web retrieval size limit.

results.finding: One GroEL complex, 14 nm in diameter, yielded a diffraction pattern with an approximate orientation.
results.detail: Orientation was estimated by matching the measured pattern to simulated patterns. The signal fell to background at about 6 nm resolution.
results.quote: GroEL which at 14 nm in diameter is the smallest biological sample ever imaged by X-rays, and demonstrate that the concept of diffraction before destruction extends to single proteins. From the pattern, it is possible to determine the approximate orientation of the protein.

results.finding: Single erythrocruorin complexes yielded diffraction patterns; 26,908 patterns were selected for 3D orientation and reconstruction.
results.detail: The iterative reconstruction estimated an orientation for each diffraction snapshot. The selected patterns were classified probabilistically.
results.quote:
During these iterations 10,395 rotation samples were modelled to 
determine the sample’s unknown orientation for each diffraction snap-shot.

results.finding: Erythrocruorin was reconstructed at approximately 20–30 Å from a selection of 26,908 single-particle patterns.
results.detail: The selected patterns were separated into 3D classes; one class was phased. The reconstruction imposed D6 symmetry, and gas-phase compaction likely limited resolution.
results.quote:
The resolution of this map is about 20 to 30 Å as determined from the 
phase-retrieval transfer function (PRTF) shown in Fig. 4 (d,e).

results.finding: Erythrocruorin was reconstructed at approximately 20–30 Å from a selection of 26,908 single-particle patterns.
results.detail: The 3D electron-density resolution is 2–3 nm, coarser than the required 1 nm.
results.quote:
The resolution of this map is about 20 to 30 Å as determined from the 
phase-retrieval transfer function (PRTF) shown in Fig. 4 (d,e).

results.finding: The merged 3D erythrocruorin intensity from 26,908 selected patterns had signal beyond 20 Å.
results.detail: The reported intensity extent does not establish sufficient sampling and integrated signal at 3 Å.
results.quote:
The signal goes beyond 20 Å resolution in the obtained 3D merged intensity (see Extended Data 
Fig. 10).

results.finding: A GroEL reconstruction from 100,000 simulated patterns reached approximately 1.1 nm resolution.
results.detail: The three-dimensional reconstruction used simulated diffraction patterns, not experimental single-copy exposures.
results.quote:
Using a 6 keV nano-focus beam and collecting
\(10^5\)
patterns, we achieved the best resolution of approximately 1.1 nm.

results.finding: A GroEL reconstruction from 100,000 simulated patterns reached approximately 1.1 nm resolution.
results.detail: The reconstruction was simulated and did not reach the sub-nanometre resolution required by the criterion.
results.quote:
Using a 6 keV nano-focus beam and collecting
\(10^5\)
patterns, we achieved the best resolution of approximately 1.1 nm.

results.finding: One non-periodic test object yielded an image with no measurable damage after a destructive 25 fs X-ray pulse.
results.detail: The image was recovered by phase retrieval from a single diffraction pattern. The object was a pattern cut into a silicon nitride membrane.
results.quote:
The reconstructed X-ray image shows no evidence of the
damage caused by the pulse.

results.finding: Photosystem I trimers: 32,788 single-particle diffraction patterns yielded a 3D electron-density map at 3.8 nm.
results.detail: The trimers were imaged in vacuum after dissolving crystals. Threefold symmetry was imposed during intensity reconstruction, but not during phasing. Detector geometry limited the reported resolution.
results.quote: The  phase  retrieval  transfer  function  remains  above  1/e  up  to  the  usable  edge  of  the  detector  (Fig.  3c),  giving  a  resolution  of  3.8  nm.
